h1: How limited edition whiskies are planned
title: How Limited Edition Whiskies Are Planned | Craft Beer School
desc: How whisky companies plan limited editions: cask selection, outturn maths, strength, numbering, allocation and protecting core range stock.
teaser: A limited edition is limited by the casks, not the marketing plan. Here is how the numbers are worked out.
standfirst: Limited editions build excitement and margin for whisky brands. They also consume stock the core range may need later. This guide explains how a release is planned, from choosing casks to deciding how many bottles each market gets.
sections:
A limited edition whisky is a release with a fixed number of bottles that will not be repeated in the same form. It might be a single cask bottling, where every bottle comes from one cask. It might be a small batch vatting of a handful of casks. Or it might be a larger annual release built around a theme, an age or a cask finish.

The limit is real because the liquid is finite. Once those casks are empty, that exact whisky is gone. Our guide to what small batch means on a whisky label explains how the terms are used.

The blender or whisky maker starts by searching the stock records for candidate casks: a particular age, a cask type such as first fill sherry or ex-bourbon, a distillation year or a warehouse. Each candidate is sampled and nosed. Some casks are outstanding. Others are fine for the core blend but would not carry a release on their own.

The key tension is with the core range. A brand's flagship 12 year old needs a steady supply of casks of that age every year. Pulling the best of those casks into a limited edition can leave the flagship short. Stock planners and blenders agree a protected volume for the core range before any limited edition casks are released.

Outturn is the number of bottles a release will yield. It starts with litres of pure alcohol (LPA), because casks differ in volume and strength.

Take a cask that now holds 180 litres at 56% ABV. That is 180 times 0.56, or 100.8 LPA.

  • Bottled at cask strength, 180 litres fills 240 bottles of 750 ml.
  • Reduced to 46% ABV, 100.8 LPA becomes about 219 litres, enough for about 292 bottles of 750 ml.

So the strength decision changes the bottle count by more than 20%. Allow for losses in filtration, line priming and quality samples, then round down. A label that says 292 bottles with only 285 good bottles off the line is an awkward conversation.

Limited editions are often bottled at cask strength or at 46% ABV or above. Many also skip chill filtration. Both choices keep more of the cask's character and both are popular with enthusiasts. Cask strength gives fewer bottles per cask. Skipping chill filtration means the whisky may turn slightly hazy when cold, which the label and the sales team should explain so it does not become a complaint. Our guide to cask strength whisky explains the trade-offs.

Numbered bottles and cask numbers on the label are part of the appeal, so the bottling run needs tight control. Labels must match the exact bottle count, cask details must match the stock records and any age statement must reflect the youngest whisky in the bottle.

Allocation decides where the bottles go. A release of 292 bottles cannot cover every state, every travel retail shop and every export market. Teams usually agree allocation by market before bottling, keeping a small reserve for press, archives and replacements for breakages. In India, each state where the release is sold needs its own label registration and price approval, which can make a small release in many states more work than it is worth.

Brands that release limited editions every year plan them years in advance. Casks are set aside or filled specially, finishes are started on schedule and the release calendar is matched against stock forecasts. That turns limited editions from a raid on the warehouse into a planned part of the portfolio.

After each release, look back at a few simple measures before planning the next. How many weeks did each market take to sell its allocation? Which markets sold out in days and which still had stock months later? Did any haze or closure complaints come in? A state that took six months to clear 30 bottles should get fewer next time, however keen its sales team sounds in the planning meeting.

Take one candidate cask from your stock records and run the outturn sum yourself: current litres, current strength, LPA and bottles at cask strength and at 46%. Then subtract 3% for losses. The result is the honest number to put in front of the brand team before anyone designs a label.
faqs: How is the number of bottles in a cask worked out?
Multiply current litres by ABV to get litres of pure alcohol. Divide by the bottling strength to get final litres, then divide by bottle size and allow for losses.
Why are limited editions often bottled at cask strength?
Cask strength keeps more of the cask's character and appeals to enthusiasts. It also means fewer bottles from each cask.
Do limited editions take stock from the core range?
They can. Stock planners usually protect a volume of each age and cask type for core brands before releasing casks for limited editions.
